msItem.note: The manuscript contains numerous later annotations, especially on the flyleaves, which deserve more detailed investigation. In the lower margin of fol. 104v, a hand writing in textualis added the poem In cratere meo Thetis est sociata Lieo (Carmina Burana 194; cf. Hugh Primas of Orléans, no. 14). In the margins of fol. 156v–157r, another textualis hand added extensive marginal notes. On fol. 160v–161r, yet another textualis hand recopied in the margins Aeneid 12.854–940.

supportDesc.support: parchment. Opening of the quires on the flesh side, with Gregory’s rule observed, except in the case of quire 4 and codicological units II, III, and IV, which open on the flesh side.
supportDesc.foliation: Modern foliation in pencil, in Arabic numerals, in the upper outer corner. From fol. 36r onwards the foliation is misnumbered by ten; the error was systematically corrected in pencil by a later hand.
supportDesc.collation:
1⁷ (fol. 1–7, fol. 3 is half sheet), 2⁶ (fol. 8–13), 3⁶ (fol. 14–19), 4² (fol. 20–21), 5⁸ (fol. 22–29), 6⁸ (fol. 30–37), 7⁸ (fol. 38–45, fol. 40 and 43 are half sheets), 8⁸ (fol. 46–53), 9³ (fol. 54–56, fol. 55 is half sheet), 10⁸ (fol. 57–64), 11⁸ (fol. 65–72, fol. 67 and 71 are half sheets), 12⁸ (fol. 73–80; fol. 74–75 form codicological unit II; fol. 78–79 form codicological unit III), 13⁸ (fol. 81–88), 14⁸ (fol. 89–96), 15⁸ (fol. 97–104), 16⁸ (fol. 105–112), 17⁸ (fol. 113–120, fol. 114 and 119 are half sheets), 18⁷ (fol. 121–127, fol. 121 is half sheet), 19⁸ (fol. 128–135, codicological unit IV; fol. 131 sheet signature “4”; quire catchword at fol. 135v), 20⁸ (fol. 136–143, codicological unit IV; quire catchword at fol. 143v), 21⁸ (fol. 144–151), 22⁷ (fol. 152–158, fol. 152 is half sheet; quire catchword at fol. 158v), 23³ (fol. 159–161).
The original structure has been disturbed by losses, displaced bifolia, and later reconstruction. Based on the current collation and after evaluating the textual gaps and signatures, we propose the following reconstruction:
Quires 2 and 3, originally quaternions, have each lost their outer bifolium. Assuming an average of 35–36 lines of text per page, the resulting textual losses correspond closely to the lacunae between quire 1 (fol. 7v, Ecl. 5.62) and quire 2 (fol. 8r, Ecl. 6.44), between quire 2 (fol. 13v, Georg. 1.53) and quire 3 (fol. 14r, Georg. 1.201), and between quire 3 (fol. 19v, Georg. 2.114) and the present quire 4 (fol. 20r, Georg. 3.294).
The much larger textual discontinuity between the end of quire 3 and the beginning of the present quire 4 has a different explanation. Two complete quires have been lost between the present quires 5 (fol. 29v, Georg. 3.221) and 6 (fol. 30r, Georg. 4.227). The present quire 4, now consisting of a single bifolium (fol. 20–21, containing Georg. 3.294–437), originally formed part of the first of these missing quires and was subsequently displaced to its current position. If this bifolium is disregarded, the textual loss between quire 3 (fol. 19v, Georg. 2.114) and quire 5 (fol. 22r, Georg. 2.188) corresponds closely to the amount of text that would have occupied the outer bifolium of quire 3.
The lacunae in quire 12 have been supplied by two additional codicological units, probably dating to the 14th century: Unit II consists of fol. 74–75 (a bifolium), and Unit III of fol. 78–79 (a bifolium).
Quires 19 and 20 form codicological Unit IV, also dated to the 14th century.
Several quires preserve ancient and more recent Roman numeral and alphabetical signatures. The only quire signature that can be considered contemporary with the text is the capital Beneventan A located at the centre of the lower margin of the verso of the last folio of the first quire; it is followed by an I (numeral), most likely of later date. Quires 2 and 3 do not bear any quire signature due to the loss of the outer bifolium. Quire 5 preserves faint traces on the lower margin of the recto of the first folio; however, on the lower margin of the verso of the last folio there appears a IIII with an abbreviation mark. The signatures of all other quires are later than the insertion of the present quire 4.
Quire 6 bears an f in Caroline script and VI (very faint; it is impossible to determine whether the two signatures are by the same hand) in the lower margin of the first folio; the sequence then continues, albeit irregularly, always on the recto of the first folio in the lower margin: quire 7 has VII; quire 8 is marked with an h in Caroline script; quire 9 is marked I VIIII, and another hand adds a caroline VIIII at the centre of the lower margin of the verso of the last folio; quire 10 is marked K on the recto of the first folio, with traces of a trimmed signature on the verso of the last folio.
From quire 11 onwards, the alphabetical sequence of signatures on the recto of the first folio remains correct (quires 11–18 marked L–R), but these are accompanied by Roman numerals (quires 11–18 marked XII–XVIII), with a discrepancy of one that cannot be explained, since there is no textual lacuna between quires 10 and 11. Codicological unit IV bears no signature; the sequence resumes at quire 21, marked in an inexplicable manner T XVI (sic) on the recto of the first folio, and concludes at quire 22, marked X XVII on the verso of the last folio.

handNote.p: Codicological unit I: Littera Beneventana, Bari type – 11th century, second half (Lowe 1914, p. 151).

At least 2 hands. The change of hand is perceptible, for example, between fol. 45v and 46r: the ink changes, and several majuscule letterforms (notably A and D) are executed in a markedly different manner. At the end of fol. 45v, the scribe had begun copying the first ten lines of Book 2 of the Aeneid. The text, however, recommences from line 1 on fol. 46r, which also marks the beginning of a new quire. This quire may therefore have been assigned to a different scribe.

At least two campaigns of Beneventan annotation can be identified in the scholia. See, for example, fol. 13r, where the main scribe added a marginal annotation in brown ink, while a second, less formal hand, writing in darker ink, added interlinear and marginal notes with reference signs, as well as making occasional corrections to the text.

provenance.p: Attached to the front paper flyleaves are two noteworthy documents. The first is a note, probably written by Matteo Luigi Canonici himself (1727-1805), stating that the manuscript had previously belonged to “N. Beccaria”, a fifteenth-century notary from Verona, who claimed to have purchased it directly from the Alighieri family as the Virgil said to have belonged to Dante. According to the document, Beccaria bequeathed it, together with other valuable manuscripts that he owned, to the “canonici regolari” of the monastery of San Leonardo, located on Monte Donico near Verona. The manuscript has been identified with entry 12 in the list of manuscripts given by Antonio Beccaria to the monastery: 'Virgilii opera uetustissima cum comento Seruii circumquaque inscripto' (Survival of Ancient Literature, no. 112, where the association with Dante is treated sceptically).

The monastery was suppressed in 1783, and its books were transferred to Venice, when Canonici most likely acquired the manuscript. This is plausibly the same Virgil codex that he described in letters written between the final months of 1783 and the beginning of 1784 to correspondents such as Giovanni Bernardo De Rossi (1742-1831), Francesco Cancellieri (1751-1826), and Ireneo Affò (1741-1797) as “lacking several leaves” yet “most beautiful and exceedingly ancient” (Irma Merolle, “L’abate Matteo Luigi Canonici. Le sue raccolte d’arte e la sua biblioteca”, Archivum Historicum Societatis Iesu 27 (1958), p. 39-40).

The second document is a letter dated January 1784 from Angelo Maria Bandini (1726-1803), librarian of the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, responding to Canonici’s doubts concerning the dating of the codex.
